prompt.context: Midwest Hospital is a research-based hospital and takes pride in its joint replacement surgery department. Recently they did a P&L analysis for all departments and found that the joint replacement surgery department is making losses. The CEO has asked for our help.
prompt.question: How would you help the CEO understand why the joint replacement surgery department is unprofitable, and what levers could be used to turn it around?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any financial targets we need to hit?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are no financial targets.

exhibits.title: Patient Mix
exhibits.shows: Breakdown of joint replacement surgeries by payer type, showing number of surgeries, list price, and invoiced price for each payer category

exhibits.title: Joint Replacement Department P&L
exhibits.shows: Income statement for the joint replacement department showing revenue, variable costs broken out by category, fixed costs broken out by category, total costs, and net profit

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmarking
exhibits.shows: Comparison of Midwest Hospital against four competitors on number of surgeries, patient mix by payer type (Commercial, HMO, Medicare), and profitability status

framework: Revenue drivers: price per surgery (by payer type) and volume/mix of surgeries
Cost drivers: variable costs (physician, materials, other) and fixed costs (facilities, other)
Patient mix analysis: evaluate profitability contribution by payer type (Commercial vs. Insurance/HMO vs. Medicare)
Competitive benchmarking: compare volume, mix, and cost structure to profitable peers
Profitability levers: increase price, shift patient mix toward higher-paying payers, grow total surgery volume, reduce costs, explore adjacent revenue streams (e.g., post-surgery physiotherapy)

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1 — Would it be advisable to stop catering to Medicare patients (assume no backlash)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate contribution margin per Medicare patient. Even though Medicare patients are unprofitable on a fully-allocated basis, they still contribute positively above variable cost, so dropping them would worsen the loss by removing their fixed-cost coverage.

math.setup: Need to calculate revenue and variable cost per patient type to assess marginal contribution. Total surgeries = 1000. Revenue from Exhibit 1 (invoiced prices): Commercial = 100 x $40K = $4M; Insurance = 300 x $20K = $6M; Medicare = 600 x $15K = $9M; Total = $19M (matches Exhibit 2). Variable costs from Exhibit 2: Total VC = $5M + $5M + $4M = $14M. Average VC per surgery = $14M / 1000 = $14K. Average revenue per surgery = $19M / 1000 = $19K. Medicare invoiced price = $15K; VC per patient = $14K; Medicare contribution margin = $15K - $14K = $1K per patient (positive).
steps: Medicare contribution margin = $15K - $14K = +$1K per surgery (above variable cost)
Dropping 600 Medicare patients would reduce revenue by $9M and reduce VC by $8.4M (600 x $14K), worsening net by $0.6M further
math.answer: Medicare patients contribute $1K above variable cost per surgery. Dropping them is NOT recommended — it would reduce fixed cost coverage and increase total losses.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 — What is the number of surgeries Midwest needs to conduct in a year to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use contribution margin per surgery and fixed costs to solve for breakeven volume. Should also calculate the implied patient mix if same proportions are maintained.

math.setup: Average revenue per surgery = $19K (from $19M / 1000). Average variable cost per surgery = $14K (from $14M / 1000). Contribution margin per surgery = $19K - $14K = $5K. Fixed costs = $3.5M + $3.5M = $7M. Breakeven = FC / CM per surgery.
steps: At same mix (10% / 30% / 60%): Commercial = 140, Insurance = 420, Medicare = 840
math.answer: 1,400 surgeries required to break even. At current mix: 140 commercial, 420 insurance, 840 Medicare.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 3 — Why is Comp D able to stay profitable despite having fewer patients and an even less favorable patient mix than Midwest (only 5% commercial, 75% Medicare)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that volume alone and mix alone do not explain Comp D's profitability. The explanation must lie in cost structure differences or better negotiated pricing. Strong candidates will note both possibilities and suggest benchmarking.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers could Midwest Hospital use to improve profitability of the joint replacement surgery department?

categories.name: Increase Revenue per Patient
ideas: Negotiate better reimbursement rates with insurance and Medicare
Shift marketing to attract more commercial (enterprise-insured) patients
Explore premium service offerings for commercial patients

categories.name: Improve Patient Mix
ideas: Increase outreach to employers with commercial insurance plans
Partner with companies to be preferred provider for joint replacement
Reduce Medicare patient share by capacity allocation if legally permissible

categories.name: Increase Total Surgery Volume
ideas: Build referral networks with primary care physicians

categories.name: Reduce Costs
ideas: Benchmark physician compensation against peers (Comp D)
Improve scheduling efficiency to lower per-surgery overhead
Reduce facilities costs through shared services or consolidation

recommendation: Midwest Hospital should NOT exit the Medicare segment — those patients still cover variable costs and contribute to fixed-cost recovery
Priority should be to grow total surgery volume (current 1,000 vs. breakeven 1,400) and to gradually shift patient mix toward higher-margin commercial and insurance patients
risks: Shifting mix away from Medicare may face regulatory or reputational constraints
Cost reduction efforts may affect care quality, which conflicts with the hospital's research-based identity
Volume growth requires capital investment in capacity
next_steps: Conduct competitive cost benchmarking against Comp D to identify specific cost reduction opportunities
Analyze pricing negotiation leverage with insurance payers to improve HMO reimbursement
Evaluate feasibility and ROI of post-surgery physiotherapy as a vertical integration play
Develop a commercial patient acquisition strategy through employer partnerships
